title: Automation scripts
subtitle: Let Python do the boring work, safely
goal: Write file automation scripts with pathlib, shutil and argparse that plan first, dry-run by default and are ready to schedule.
outcomes: Scan and organise folders with pathlib and shutil
Separate planning from acting, with a dry-run default
Build typed command-line interfaces with argparse
Rename files in bulk without collisions or overwrites
Schedule scripts with cron, Task Scheduler or CI

slides.title: Mission 51: Automation scripts
slides.body:
Professionals automate anything they do twice: sorting downloads, renaming 500 photos, a report every Monday.

Today you write scripts that touch **real files safely**: plan first, dry-run by default, then let them run on a schedule.

items: Spot a boring task you repeat
Script it: find, decide, act, report

slides.say: Welcome to phase six, Pro. Developers automate anything they do twice: sorting a messy downloads folder, renaming five hundred photos, sending a report every Monday. Today you write automation scripts that work on real files, and you build them the safe way: plan first, dry run by default, then schedule them to run without you.

slides.title: Anatomy of an automation script
slides.body:
Almost every file script has the same four parts:
- **Find** the files (`pathlib`)
- **Decide** what to do with each (a plain function)
- **Act** (`shutil`, `Path.rename`), but only when asked
- **Report** what happened

nodes.t: For each file: decide its destination

slides.say: Almost every automation script has four parts. Find the files, decide what to do with each one, act on that decision, and report what happened. The safest scripts separate deciding from acting, so you can always see the plan before a single file moves.

slides.title: Scan a folder with pathlib
slides.body: A virtual `downloads` folder sits next to this program. `iterdir()` lists what is inside; `stat()` gives file details such as size.

budget.xlsx          .xlsx     900 bytes

iterdir() lists the folder; sorted() makes the order predictable.
Subfolders are reported, not treated as files.
stat().st_size is the file size in bytes.
suffix is the extension; lower() makes .PDF and .pdf the same.

slides.say: This folder is a typical downloads mess. We loop over everything inside it, sorted so the output is stable. For folders we print a slash. For files we print the name, the extension in lower case, and the size in bytes from stat. Notice the upper case dot J P G and dot P D F: real folders are never tidy.

slides.title: Path pieces you will use daily
slides.body: A `Path` splits a file name into useful parts, so you never slice strings by hand.
slides.say: A Path object hands you every piece of a file name. Name is the full file name, stem is the name without the extension, suffix is the extension, and parent is the folder it lives in. with suffix and with name build new paths, which is exactly what batch renaming needs.

slides.title: Predict the pieces
slides.code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("reports/2026/sales.final.csv")
print(p.stem, p.suffix, p.parent.name)
slides.why: suffix is only the last extension, `.csv`, so the stem keeps `sales.final`. `parent` is the folder `reports/2026`, and its `.name` is just `2026`.
slides.say: A file name with two dots. What do stem, suffix and the parent's name print? Think about which dot the suffix starts from.

slides.title: Decide first: a pure planning function
slides.body: The rules are data (a dict), and the decision is a pure function: no files touched, easy to test.
slides.expect:
invoice.pdf    -> Documents
IMG_2041.JPG   -> Images
song.mp3       -> Music
setup.exe      -> Other
explain: Rules as data: add a category by adding a line.
get() with a default: unknown extensions go to Other.
Try names only: no real files needed to test the logic.
slides.say: The decision lives in one small function that touches no files at all. It looks up the lower case extension in a dictionary and falls back to Other. Because it is pure, it is trivial to test, and changing the rules means editing one dictionary.

slides.title: Act: move files with shutil, dry run by default
slides.body: `dry_run=True` is the **default**. The script must be asked explicitly to change anything.
slides.expect:

would move report.PDF -> Documents/

['Documents', 'Images', 'Music', 'Other', 'archive']
explain: Safe default: dry_run is True unless the caller says otherwise.
Build the target path with the / operator.
Record the action whether or not we perform it.

slides.say: Here is the full organiser. It always builds the list of actions, but it only creates folders and moves files when dry run is false. The default is true, so forgetting a flag can never wreck a folder. We print the plan first, then apply it, then list the folder: four tidy category folders, and the old archive left alone.

slides.title: Quick check: safety first
slides.q: Your organiser has a bug that sends every file to the wrong folder. Which design limits the damage most?
options: Run it on your real Downloads folder and check afterwards
Default to a dry run that prints the plan; only move files with an explicit flag
Wrap every move in `try/except` and ignore errors
Add more comments explaining the moves
slides.why: A dry run shows the plan before anything changes, so you catch the bug by reading. Swallowing errors hides problems; it does not prevent them.
slides.say: Imagine your organiser has a bug that sends every file to the wrong place. Which design protects you best?

slides.title: argparse: a real command-line interface
slides.body: Real scripts take options from the terminal. `argparse` reads them, converts types, rejects bad input and writes `--help` for you.

lines: DRY RUN: 6 files would move (add --apply to move them)

slides.say: Real tools take options from the command line, like a folder name or an apply flag. The argparse module reads those options, converts them to the right types, rejects nonsense with a clear message, and even writes the help screen for you. This is how professional Python command line tools are built.

slides.title: Build the parser
slides.body: On a laptop, `parse_args()` reads the real command line. Passing a list, as here, is how you **test** a CLI.
slides.code:
import argparse

def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="organise", description="Sort files by type.")
    parser.add_argument("folder", help="folder to organise")
    parser.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true", help="really move files")
    parser.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=0, help="stop after N files")
    return parser

parser = build_parser()
print(parser.format_usage(), end="")

args = parser.parse_args(["downloads"])
print(args)

args = parser.parse_args(["downloads", "--apply", "--limit", "10"])
print(args.folder, args.apply, args.limit, type(args.limit).__name__)
slides.expect:
usage: organise [-h] [--apply] [--limit LIMIT] folder
Namespace(folder='downloads', apply=False, limit=0)
downloads True 10 int
explain: A positional argument: required, no dashes.
store_true: a flag that is False unless present.
type=int converts the text '10' to the number 10.
argparse writes the usage line for you.
Parse a pretend command line.
slides.say: We describe the interface once: a required folder, an apply flag that is false unless given, and a limit that argparse converts to an integer. On your laptop, parse args reads the real command line. Here we pass a list ourselves, which is exactly how you test a command line tool.

slides.title: Fix the bug: the dry run that wasn't
slides.task: This batch renamer should only **plan** when `dry_run` is true. Run it: the photos get renamed anyway. Fix it so a dry run touches nothing, while `dry_run=False` really renames.
slides.starter:
from pathlib import Path

def add_prefix(folder: Path, prefix: str, dry_run: bool = True) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    planned = []
    for path in sorted(folder.glob("*.jpg")):
        new_path = path.with_name(prefix + path.name)
        planned.append((path.name, new_path.name))
        if dry_run:
            path.rename(new_path)
    return planned

print(add_prefix(Path("photos"), "goa_"))
print(sorted(p.name for p in Path("photos").iterdir()))
slides.solution:
from pathlib import Path

def add_prefix(folder: Path, prefix: str, dry_run: bool = True) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    planned = []
    for path in sorted(folder.glob("*.jpg")):
        new_path = path.with_name(prefix + path.name)
        planned.append((path.name, new_path.name))
        if not dry_run:
            path.rename(new_path)
    return planned

print(add_prefix(Path("photos"), "goa_"))
print(sorted(p.name for p in Path("photos").iterdir()))
slides.tests:
from pathlib import Path
folder = Path("photos")
names = sorted(p.name for p in folder.iterdir())
assert names == ["IMG_01.jpg", "IMG_02.jpg", "notes.txt"], "A dry run must not touch any file, but the folder now holds " + str(names) + ". Look at the if before rename()."
plan = add_prefix(folder, "goa_")
assert plan == [("IMG_01.jpg", "goa_IMG_01.jpg"), ("IMG_02.jpg", "goa_IMG_02.jpg")], "The dry run should still return the plan of (old, new) names."
add_prefix(folder, "goa_", dry_run=False)
names = sorted(p.name for p in folder.iterdir())
assert names == ["goa_IMG_01.jpg", "goa_IMG_02.jpg", "notes.txt"], "With dry_run=False the photos should really be renamed. The folder holds " + str(names)
hints: Read the condition before `path.rename` out loud. When should renaming happen?
Only rename when it is **not** a dry run: `if not dry_run:`
slides.say: Here is a classic, dangerous bug. This renamer is supposed to only plan when dry run is true, but run it and look at the folder: the photos were renamed anyway. Find the line that decides when to rename, and fix it so a dry run never touches a file.

slides.title: Batch renaming without regrets
slides.body:
Rules for any script that renames or moves many files:
- **Plan all new names first**, then apply
- **Check for collisions**: two files must never get the same name
- **Never overwrite**: skip or stop if the target exists
- **Idempotent**: running twice gives the same result
- **Log** every change so you can undo it

right.title: Safe

visual.verdict: Plan, check, then act: a bug shows up in the plan, not in your photo library.

slides.say: Renaming many files is where scripts do real damage. Plan every new name before touching anything. Check that no two files end up with the same name, and never overwrite an existing file. Make the script idempotent, which means running it twice gives the same result as running it once. And log every change, so you can undo it.

slides.title: Generate a report
slides.body: `rglob("*")` walks every subfolder too. The report is built as a list of lines and written in one go.
slides.code:
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("downloads")
counts, sizes = Counter(), Counter()
for path in sorted(folder.rglob("*")):
    if path.is_file():
        kind = path.suffix.lower() or "(none)"
        counts[kind] += 1
        sizes[kind] += path.stat().st_size

lines = [f"Folder report: {folder}", "-" * 32]
for kind, n in counts.most_common():
    lines.append(f"{kind:<7} {n:>2} file(s) {sizes[kind]:>8,} bytes")
lines.append(f"{'total':<7} {counts.total():>2} file(s) {sizes.total():>8,} bytes")

report = Path("report.txt")
report.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(report.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), end="")
slides.expect:
Folder report: downloads
--------------------------------
.pdf     2 file(s)    2,001 bytes
.jpg     1 file(s)    2,400 bytes
.zip     1 file(s)    4,000 bytes
.xlsx    1 file(s)      900 bytes
.txt     1 file(s)       51 bytes
.mp3     1 file(s)    3,000 bytes
total    7 file(s)   12,352 bytes
explain: rglob searches recursively; sorted keeps the order stable.
Files without an extension get a readable label.
most_common() sorts by count, biggest first.
Write the whole report at once, with an explicit encoding.

files.downloads/notes.txt:
Buy chai patti
Call the plumber
Renew Tatkal login

slides.say: Automation often ends with a report. rglob walks the folder and every subfolder. Two counters track how many files of each type we found and how many bytes they use. We build the lines in a list, join them once, write the report to a file and print it back. Swap the print for an email and this is a Monday morning report.

slides.title: Your turn: the organiser

slides.tests:
from pathlib import Path
inbox = Path("inbox")
before = sorted(p.name for p in inbox.iterdir())
plan = organise(inbox)
expected = [("beach.jpg", "Images"), ("notes.txt", "Documents"), ("report.PDF", "Documents"), ("setup.exe", "Other"), ("song.mp3", "Music")]
assert plan == expected, "The dry-run plan should be " + str(expected) + " but it was " + str(plan) + ". Check lower-case extensions, the Other fallback and skipping folders."
assert sorted(p.name for p in inbox.iterdir()) == before, "A dry run must not move anything. Only move files when apply is True."
organise(inbox, apply=True)
for rel in ["Images/beach.jpg", "Documents/notes.txt", "Documents/report.PDF", "Other/setup.exe", "Music/song.mp3", "old/keep.txt"]:
    assert (inbox / rel).is_file(), "After apply=True, inbox/" + rel + " should exist. Create the category folder, then move the file into it."
assert organise(inbox, apply=True) == [], "Running it a second time should find no loose files and return an empty list."
hints: Inside `if apply:` use `(folder / category).mkdir(exist_ok=True)` then `shutil.move(path, folder / category / path.name)`.
slides.say: Now build the organiser yourself. Skip folders, pick each file's category from the rules using its lower case extension, and return the plan as a list of name and category pairs. Only when apply is true should it create folders and move files. The tests also run it twice, so make sure a second run is harmless.

slides.title: Scheduling: let it run without you
slides.body:
A script you must remember to run is only half automated. Schedulers run it for you.

Scheduled scripts run with **no one watching**: use absolute paths, log to a file, and exit with a non-zero code when something fails.
slides.say: A script you have to remember to run is only half automated. On Linux and Mac, cron runs commands on a schedule. On Windows, Task Scheduler does the same. In the cloud, GitHub Actions and similar tools can run your script every night. Remember that nobody is watching: use absolute paths, write logs to a file, and exit with an error code when something fails.

slides.title: Read a cron schedule
slides.q: Cron fields are: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week (0 = Sunday). When does this line run?
options: On the 5th of every month at 6:30 pm
slides.why: Minute 30, hour 18, any day of the month, any month, day of week 5 (Friday). So: 18:30 every Friday.
slides.say: Cron uses five fields: minute, hour, day of the month, month, and day of the week. Read this line field by field. When will the script run?

slides.solution:
import argparse

def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="rename", description="Batch-rename files safely.")
    parser.add_argument("folder", help="folder with the files")
    parser.add_argument("--prefix", required=True, help="text to put before each name")
    parser.add_argument("--ext", default=".jpg", help="only rename files with this extension")
    parser.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true", help="really rename (default: dry run)")
    parser.add_argument("--start", type=int, default=1, help="first number to use")
    return parser

print(build_parser().format_usage(), end="")
hints: A flag is `action="store_true"`; a number is `type=int, default=1`.
slides.say: Your turn to design a command line. Finish the parser for a rename tool: a required prefix, an extension that defaults to dot j p g, an apply flag, and a start number that must arrive as an integer. The tests even check that forgetting the prefix makes argparse stop with an error.

You can scan folders with pathlib, separate deciding from acting, move and rename files safely with a dry run by default, build a proper command line with argparse, and schedule scripts to run on their own.
